// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

firmwareCode:
// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

firmwareCode:
// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

firmwareCode:
// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

description.objective: Implementación y validación técnica de Cold-Gas Reaction Thruster.
description.purpose:
Out in orbit there is nothing to push against, so spacecraft change and hold their orientation by firing
small thrusters — the reaction control system (RCS). You can build the same thing on the ground:
mount a platform on a near-frictionless bearing, plumb a few small solenoid valves to a
compressed-gas supply, and fire short puffs to rotate it and hold a commanded heading. An IMU
senses the angle, a controller decides which thruster to pulse and for how long, and the platform slews
and stops on target — no wheels, no contact, just gas. This is exactly how satellites maneuver, and the
air-bearing version is literally how aerospace labs test real attitude-control hardware before flight. It is
the most viscerally 'spacecraft' project you can build on a bench.

// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

evidenceBlocks.textSnippet:
A satellite in low orbit crosses the sky in minutes, so to keep a high-gain antenna pointed at it you need
a tracker that moves. This project builds a real azimuth-elevation rotator: two motors aim an antenna, a
microcontroller predicts the satellite's position from its orbital elements, and the antenna physically
slews to follow the pass from horizon to horizon — exactly what a professional ground station does.
Pair it with an SDR and you can hold a lock on a fast-moving satellite and pull down a clean signal a
fixed antenna would lose in seconds. It is the ground half of every space mission, and watching your
antenna hunt across the sky on its own is genuinely striking.

// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

description.summary:
PROJECT 3
Magnetorquer Detumble System | When a CubeSat is ejected from its deployer it is tumbling, and before it can do anything useful it has
to stop spinning and stabilize — a maneuver called detumbling. The clever part: it has nothing to push

description.whatDoesItDo:
When a CubeSat is ejected from its deployer it is tumbling, and before it can do anything useful it has
to stop spinning and stabilize — a maneuver called detumbling. The clever part: it has nothing to push
against, so it pushes against Earth itself. Electromagnets called magnetorquers create a magnetic
moment that interacts with Earth's magnetic field to produce a tiny torque, bleeding off the spin. This
project builds exactly that: coils on a platform, a magnetometer to sense rotation, and the famous
'B-dot' control law that drives the coils to kill the tumble. It is one of the most elegant ideas in spacecraft
engineering — steering against a planet's magnetic field — and it is genuinely buildable and cheap.

When a CubeSat is ejected from its deployer it is tumbling, and before it can do anything useful it has
to stop spinning and stabilize — a maneuver called detumbling. The clever part: it has nothing to push
against, so it pushes against Earth itself. Electromagnets called magnetorquers create a magnetic
moment that interacts with Earth's magnetic field to produce a tiny torque, bleeding off the spin. This
project builds exactly that: coils on a platform, a magnetometer to sense rotation, and the famous
'B-dot' control law that drives the coils to kill the tumble. It is one of the most elegant ideas in spacecraft
engineering — steering against a planet's magnetic field — and it is genuinely buildable and cheap.

firmwareCode:
// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

evidenceBlocks.claim: Arquitectura y topología de CubeSat Flight Computer (OBC).
evidenceBlocks.textSnippet:
Every spacecraft has a brain: the command-and-data-handling (C&DH;) computer that reads the
sensors, runs the housekeeping, packages everything into telemetry, and beams it to the ground while
accepting commands back up. This project builds a working one — a flight-computer stack that
samples its sensors, forms proper telemetry packets, transmits them over a radio link to a ground
station you also build, and decodes them onto a live dashboard. Use the real spacecraft data standard
(CCSDS) for the packets and you have built the same data architecture that flies on actual missions. It
is less flashy than a thruster, but it is the literal nervous system of a satellite — and the flight-software
skill is in high demand.

firmwareCode:
// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

evidenceBlocks.textSnippet:
To point itself, a spacecraft first has to know which way it is facing — and the simplest, cheapest,
most-flown way to get a reference is to find the Sun. A sun sensor measures the direction to the Sun in
the spacecraft's own frame, and that single vector is enough to constrain attitude for power-positioning
and coarse pointing. This project builds a real one: an arrangement of photodiodes (or a pinhole over a
small sensor array) whose relative readings encode the Sun's angle, plus the math to turn those
readings into a sun vector. It is a clean, satisfying sensor project — analog front end, geometry, and
calibration — and it is a genuine flight sensor, not a toy.

// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

evidenceBlocks.textSnippet:
A satellite lives and dies by its power system. The EPS (electrical power subsystem) harvests energy
from solar panels, charges and protects the battery, regulates it into the voltage rails every other
subsystem needs, and reports power health as telemetry — all of it autonomously, because there is no
one to flip a switch in orbit. This project builds a real one: a solar input stage that charges a lithium
battery safely, regulated output rails, protection against over-current and over-discharge, and
voltage/current telemetry on every channel. It is the same architecture as a flight EPS, and it is the
subsystem that keeps everything else alive — which is exactly why power engineers are always in
demand.

firmwareCode:
// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

evidenceBlocks.claim: Componentes críticos de TPMS Car-ID Sniffer.
evidenceBlocks.textSnippet:
Every modern car has tire-pressure sensors that periodically transmit on 315 MHz (North America) or
433 MHz (Europe) — and each transmission includes a unique sensor ID along with pressure and
temperature. They are unencrypted and broadcast whenever the wheels turn, which means a cheap
radio can log them. Researchers have shown TPMS IDs can be used to identify and track vehicles, and
this project lets you see that privacy gap with your own eyes: park near a road, decode the packets,
and watch unique IDs roll past. It is a striking lesson in how much our everyday devices leak — and
exactly the kind of wireless-security insight that automotive and IoT-security teams hire for.

Every modern car has tire-pressure sensors that periodically transmit on 315 MHz (North America) or
433 MHz (Europe) — and each transmission includes a unique sensor ID along with pressure and
temperature. They are unencrypted and broadcast whenever the wheels turn, which means a cheap
radio can log them. Researchers have shown TPMS IDs can be used to identify and track vehicles, and
this project lets you see that privacy gap with your own eyes: park near a road, decode the packets,
and watch unique IDs roll past. It is a striking lesson in how much our everyday devices leak — and
exactly the kind of wireless-security insight that automotive and IoT-security teams hire for.

// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

evidenceBlocks.textSnippet:
When a meteor streaks through the upper atmosphere it leaves a trail of ionized gas that briefly reflects
radio waves — and you can hear it. By tuning to a powerful distant VHF transmitter that is normally
below your horizon (a dedicated radar like GRAVES, or a far-off TV or FM carrier), you receive
nothing... until a meteor trail bounces that signal over the horizon to your antenna, producing a sudden
'ping.' This is forward-scatter meteor detection, and it works day or night, through clouds, even when
you cannot see a thing. You are detecting objects from space by their effect on radio propagation —
real radio-astronomy technique, built from a $30 dongle and a simple antenna.

firmwareCode:
// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

evidenceBlocks.textSnippet:
The 433 MHz ISM band is full of chatter you never notice: wireless weather stations, remote
thermometers, soil-moisture sensors, doorbells, garage remotes, and cheap smart-home gadgets all
transmit there in the clear. Point an SDR at it and an open-source decoder turns that noise into
readable data — temperatures, humidity, button presses, sensor IDs — from devices all around your
neighbourhood and inside your own home. It is the most approachable possible introduction to IoT
reverse-engineering, and the natural gateway to building your own sensor network or auditing what
your devices leak. The same skills underpin IoT product development and wireless security.

firmwareCode:
// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

evidenceBlocks.claim: Principio físico y lógico de Stratospheric Radiosonde Tracker.
evidenceBlocks.textSnippet:
Twice a day, from hundreds of sites worldwide, weather agencies launch balloons carrying
radiosondes — small instrument packages that transmit temperature, humidity, pressure, and GPS
position as they rise to ~30 km, then parachute back to Earth. Those transmissions (around 400-406
MHz) are unencrypted, so you can receive a sonde's live telemetry, plot its track, and — using its GPS
position and a descent model — predict where it will land and go recover it. It is a genuine treasure
hunt powered by RF: decode a real aerospace telemetry stream, do the tracking and prediction math,
and end up holding the instrument you tracked from the edge of space. Recovered sondes are also
reusable for your own high-altitude projects.

firmwareCode:
// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

description.purpose:
The control loop: Each cycle you compute error = target − measured, turn that error into a
motor command, apply it, and repeat hundreds to thousands of times a second. The faster and
more regular the loop, the tighter the control.
description.summary:
❯ project 02
Closed-Loop Position Servo | BUILD NOTE
Reach for a microcontroller with a fast, regular loop and a real quadrature input.
Decode the encoder cleanly first and confirm the count tracks the shaft before you close
any loop — a flaky encoder makes PID impossible to tune.

evidenceBlocks.claim: Arquitectura y topología de Field-Oriented Control (FOC) BLDC Servo.
evidenceBlocks.textSnippet:
Open-loop, a motor just spins and you have no idea where it actually is. Add an encoder to
measure its position and a PID controller to drive the error to zero, and the motor becomes a
servo: command 90 degrees and it snaps there and holds, resisting if you push it. This is the
single most important skill in motor control and robotics — closing the loop with feedback —
and it is the foundation under every robot joint, CNC axis, and drone. Building your own PID
position controller (rather than buying a servo) is the project that turns “I can spin a
motor” into “I can control motion.”

evidenceBlocks.claim: Seguridad operativa y protecciones de Field-Oriented Control (FOC) BLDC Servo.
evidenceBlocks.textSnippet:
Why add the integral term if P almost works? Proportional control alone leaves a residual
error — the motor settles where P’s push balances friction and load, short of the target.
The integral term accumulates that leftover error until it is driven to zero, so the servo
actually reaches the commanded angle and holds it under load.

the target tilt — so the robot not only balances but holds its ground (or drives where

description.whatDoesItDo:
A two-wheel balancing robot is an inverted pendulum: left alone it falls, so it only stays
upright because a controller is constantly catching it. An IMU measures the tilt, a control
loop computes how to drive the wheels to stay under the centre of mass, and the robot
balances — leaning into a push and recovering. It is the most visually striking build in this
guide and a genuine lesson in controlling an unstable system, sensor fusion, and cascaded
control. If the closed-loop servo taught you to hold a position, this teaches you to
stabilise something that actively wants to fall.

firmwareCode:
// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

evidenceBlocks.textSnippet:
Brushless (BLDC / PMSM) motors are everywhere high performance matters — drones, EVs, robot
joints, gimbals — because they are efficient, powerful, and long-lived. But they need
electronic commutation: you must energise the right coils at the right instant based on rotor
position. Field-Oriented Control (FOC) does this optimally, producing smooth, silent, full-
torque-at-any-speed motion, even holding still. Building a FOC drive — with a position
sensor, a three-phase driver, and a library like SimpleFOC — is the leap into modern motor
control and one of the most in-demand EE skills in robotics and electrified everything.

electronic commutation: you must energise the right coils at the right instant based on rotor
position. Field-Oriented Control (FOC) does this optimally, producing smooth, silent, full-
torque-at-any-speed motion, even holding still. Building a FOC drive — with a position
sensor, a three-phase driver, and a library like SimpleFOC — is the leap into modern motor
control and one of the most in-demand EE skills in robotics and electrified everything.

// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

multi-axis coordination, a different and essential facet of motor control.

firmwareCode:
// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

DO THIS
Build even one. Film it — a motor snapping to a target and resisting your push, a robot
catching itself, a brushless motor holding torque in silence, a machine drawing — and
put the code on GitHub with the control loop, your tuning, and an honest note on what
works and what doesn’t. One motion demo and one clean repo prove you can make hardware
do exactly what you tell it.

description.whatDoesItDo:
Most knobs are passive; this one fights back. By driving a brushless motor with FOC and
reading its exact angle, you can render torque as a function of position — so the same
physical knob can feel like clicky detents, a smooth spring that returns to centre, or a hard
end-stop, all changed in software. It is the technology behind high-end car controls and the
viral “smart knob,” and it is a brilliant lesson in torque control and haptics: you are
programming a force field you can feel with your fingers. It builds directly on FOC and turns
motor control into a user interface.

physical knob can feel like clicky detents, a smooth spring that returns to centre, or a hard
end-stop, all changed in software. It is the technology behind high-end car controls and the
viral “smart knob,” and it is a brilliant lesson in torque control and haptics: you are
programming a force field you can feel with your fingers. It builds directly on FOC and turns
motor control into a user interface.

// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

description.whatDoesItDo:
Every drone company assumes a graduate has only ever flashed Betaflight, and that assumption
is usually correct. This project forces you through the part the firmware hides: raw gyro
rates and accelerometer vectors coming in at 1 kHz, a complementary (or Kalman) filter turning
them into a roll and pitch angle, and a PID loop turning that angle error into motor commands.
You will discover that the textbook loop oscillates on a real rig, that the gyro drifts, that
the accelerometer lies under vibration, and that the difference between a stable hover and a
flip is a derivative term and a 100 Hz low-pass filter. Debugging that on a hinged one-axis
test stand, with a logged plot of setpoint versus measured angle, is the actual skill a
flight-controls engineer is hired for.

// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

evidenceBlocks.claim: Arquitectura y topología de High-Speed Brushless ESC.
evidenceBlocks.textSnippet:
An ESC is a black box to most EE students: a $12 brick that turns a PWM signal into a spinning
motor. Inside it is a three-phase half-bridge, gate drivers, a microcontroller and a way of
finding the rotor without sensors — by watching the back-EMF zero crossing on the floating
phase. Building it yourself means you will blow a MOSFET by shooting through a half-bridge,
you will see the back-EMF on a scope and learn why it only appears once the motor is already
turning, and you will write an open-loop start-up ramp that hands off to sensorless
commutation. That is the exact circuit inside every motor controller in the industry, and the
debugging — dead time, gate charge, current spikes — is the actual job.

firmwareCode:
// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

evidenceBlocks.claim: Puesta en marcha y verificación de Bidirectional Telemetry Link.
evidenceBlocks.textSnippet:
Every drone beyond toy range needs a telemetry downlink, and every drone company has an RF
person who owns it. This project gives you the whole chain: a GPS module and a LoRa radio on
the airframe, a matching radio on a ground station, a packet format you designed, and a range
test you actually ran. You will learn why LoRa trades bit rate for sensitivity, what a link
budget is when you compute it from transmit power, antenna gain and receiver sensitivity, and
why the first range test fails at 300 m because the antenna is lying flat against a carbon
arm. The logged RSSI-versus-distance plot from a walk test is the kind of evidence an RF
hiring manager reads in five seconds.

Every drone beyond toy range needs a telemetry downlink, and every drone company has an RF
person who owns it. This project gives you the whole chain: a GPS module and a LoRa radio on
the airframe, a matching radio on a ground station, a packet format you designed, and a range
test you actually ran. You will learn why LoRa trades bit rate for sensitivity, what a link
budget is when you compute it from transmit power, antenna gain and receiver sensitivity, and
why the first range test fails at 300 m because the antenna is lying flat against a carbon
arm. The logged RSSI-versus-distance plot from a walk test is the kind of evidence an RF
hiring manager reads in five seconds.

firmwareCode:
// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

evidenceBlocks.claim: Instrucciones de ensamblaje de Power Distribution Board & Shunt Monitor.
evidenceBlocks.textSnippet:
A gimbal is a control loop you can see working: the camera stays level while you tilt the
handle. Under that are two things a drone company cares about — sinusoidal open-loop drive of
a brushless motor (three PWM sine waves 120° apart, no commutation sensors) and a fast PID
loop closing on an IMU mounted on the camera plate itself. You will learn why the IMU must be
on the payload and not the frame, why a 400 Hz loop with a 20 Hz plant still jitters if your
PWM frequency is audible, and why the motor gets hot at standstill. The result is a two-axis
rig holding a horizon in a video you can post, plus the logged angle error that proves it.

firmwareCode:
// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

evidenceBlocks.claim: Componentes críticos de Attitude Sensor Fusion Engine.
evidenceBlocks.textSnippet:
Batteries decide flight time and batteries cause crashes, so every drone company has someone
who owns the power module. This project is that module: a shunt resistor and current-sense
amplifier for pack current, a resistor-divider per cell into a multiplexed ADC for cell
voltages, and firmware that integrates current into mAh consumed and flags a weak cell. You
will learn why a 0.5 m� shunt needs a 50 V/V amplifier, why the divider ratio matters for ADC
resolution, why cell voltage under load and at rest are different numbers, and why mAh
consumed is a better land-now signal than voltage. The logged discharge curve you produce is
the first thing a battery engineer asks for.

Batteries decide flight time and batteries cause crashes, so every drone company has someone
who owns the power module. This project is that module: a shunt resistor and current-sense
amplifier for pack current, a resistor-divider per cell into a multiplexed ADC for cell
voltages, and firmware that integrates current into mAh consumed and flags a weak cell. You
will learn why a 0.5 m� shunt needs a 50 V/V amplifier, why the divider ratio matters for ADC
resolution, why cell voltage under load and at rest are different numbers, and why mAh
consumed is a better land-now signal than voltage. The logged discharge curve you produce is
the first thing a battery engineer asks for.

firmwareCode:
// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

evidenceBlocks.claim: Instrucciones de ensamblaje de High-Rate SPI Blackbox Logger.
evidenceBlocks.textSnippet:
Indoor drones are the fastest-growing part of the industry — warehouse inventory, tunnel and
tank inspection — and none of them have GPS. This project is the answer those teams actually
use: ultra-wideband ranging. Three ESP32 + DW1000 anchors on tripods, one tag on the airframe,
two-way ranging that times a radio pulse round trip to nanoseconds, and trilateration that
turns three distances into an x/y position on a laptop map. You will learn why UWB can range
to centimetres when WiFi cannot, why antenna delay calibration is the whole game, and why
three anchors give you a position but four give you a sanity check. The logged position trace
as you walk a square is proof you can build a localization system, not just call a library.

firmwareCode:
// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

evidenceBlocks.textSnippet:
GOES (Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites) are the spacecraft behind every weather
forecast you have ever seen. They sit in geostationary orbit 35,786 km above the equator, locked to
one spot on Earth, and continuously broadcast imagery back down on an L-band downlink near 1.69
GHz. The operational satellites — GOES-19 (East) and GOES-18 (West) — transmit a signal called
HRIT that anyone can receive with a software-defined radio, a low-noise amplifier, and a dish you can
build from hardware-store parts. Because the satellite never moves relative to the ground, you aim your
antenna once and leave it — no tracking motor. The challenge is pure RF: the signal arrives near the
thermal noise floor after a 36,000 km trip, so the whole link budget hinges on a clean, low-noise front
end and enough antenna gain to close the link.

evidenceBlocks.textSnippet:
GOES (Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites) are the spacecraft behind every weather
forecast you have ever seen. They sit in geostationary orbit 35,786 km above the equator, locked to
one spot on Earth, and continuously broadcast imagery back down on an L-band downlink near 1.69
GHz. The operational satellites — GOES-19 (East) and GOES-18 (West) — transmit a signal called
HRIT that anyone can receive with a software-defined radio, a low-noise amplifier, and a dish you can
build from hardware-store parts. Because the satellite never moves relative to the ground, you aim your
antenna once and leave it — no tracking motor. The challenge is pure RF: the signal arrives near the
thermal noise floor after a 36,000 km trip, so the whole link budget hinges on a clean, low-noise front
end and enough antenna gain to close the link.

// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

evidenceBlocks.textSnippet:
For years, the way most people received their first satellite image was the NOAA APT signal on 137
MHz — but in 2025 the last NOAA APT satellite was decommissioned and that signal went silent for
good. The torch has passed to the Russian Meteor-M series, whose M2-3 and M2-4 satellites transmit
a sharper, digital signal called LRPT in the same easy-to-reach 137 MHz band. Unlike geostationary
GOES, these are polar-orbiting satellites in low Earth orbit, sweeping over your location a few times a
day and painting a strip of the planet beneath them. The whole receive chain costs about the price of a
textbook: an RTL-SDR, a simple antenna you can build from two pieces of wire, and free software. It is
the most accessible image-from-space project that still actually works in 2026.

// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

firmwareCode:
// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

evidenceBlocks.claim: Puesta en marcha y verificación de GPS-Disciplined Oscillator (GPSDO).
evidenceBlocks.textSnippet:
Every GPS satellite carries an atomic clock, and the timing signal it broadcasts is disciplined to within
nanoseconds of the global time standard. A GPS-disciplined oscillator borrows that accuracy: it takes
the once-per-second pulse (1PPS) from a cheap GPS receiver and uses it to steer a local crystal
oscillator so its frequency is locked, long-term, to atomic precision — parts-per-billion or better. This is
the quiet workhorse of every serious RF lab, cellular base station, and test bench: the reference that
everything else is measured against. Building one teaches you precision timing, control loops, and the
discipline of measuring frequency accurately — and it is the most affordable project in this guide.

evidenceBlocks.textSnippet:
Every GPS satellite carries an atomic clock, and the timing signal it broadcasts is disciplined to within
nanoseconds of the global time standard. A GPS-disciplined oscillator borrows that accuracy: it takes
the once-per-second pulse (1PPS) from a cheap GPS receiver and uses it to steer a local crystal
oscillator so its frequency is locked, long-term, to atomic precision — parts-per-billion or better. This is
the quiet workhorse of every serious RF lab, cellular base station, and test bench: the reference that
everything else is measured against. Building one teaches you precision timing, control loops, and the
discipline of measuring frequency accurately — and it is the most affordable project in this guide.

// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

evidenceBlocks.claim: Limitaciones técnicas de Cosmic-Ray Muon Detector.
evidenceBlocks.textSnippet:
Right now, particles created when cosmic rays from exploding stars and distant galaxies slam into the
upper atmosphere are raining down through your body — about one muon through every square
centimeter every minute. You can build an instrument that catches them. When a muon passes through
a plastic scintillator it leaves a tiny flash of light; a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) turns that flash into an
electrical pulse, a fast amplifier boosts it, and a discriminator counts it. This is real particle-physics
instrumentation — the same detection principle used at CERN — built on your bench for under $80. It
is also the deepest analog challenge in this guide: catching a microsecond flash of a few hundred
photons demands genuinely low-noise, high-speed front-end design.

evidenceBlocks.textSnippet:
Right now, particles created when cosmic rays from exploding stars and distant galaxies slam into the
upper atmosphere are raining down through your body — about one muon through every square
centimeter every minute. You can build an instrument that catches them. When a muon passes through
a plastic scintillator it leaves a tiny flash of light; a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) turns that flash into an
electrical pulse, a fast amplifier boosts it, and a discriminator counts it. This is real particle-physics
instrumentation — the same detection principle used at CERN — built on your bench for under $80. It
is also the deepest analog challenge in this guide: catching a microsecond flash of a few hundred
photons demands genuinely low-noise, high-speed front-end design.

firmwareCode:
// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

description.objective: Implementación y validación técnica de EMG Muscle-Controlled Prosthetic Trigger.
description.purpose:
Your body produces electrical signals measured in millivolts — and it also acts as an antenna
that picks up the mains hum flooding every room, often a thousand times larger than the
signal you want. The instrumentation amplifier is the circuit that solves this: it amplifies
only the difference between two electrodes while rejecting everything they see in common. Add
a driven-reference electrode and careful filtering and suddenly a heartbeat or a muscle
twitch emerges from the noise. This is the single circuit that makes ECG, EMG, and EEG
possible, and building it yourself — rather than buying a module — is what separates people
who understand biosignals from people who plug in a breakout board.

description.whatDoesItDo:
! BATTERY POWER, ALWAYS — AND NEVER INJECT CURRENT
Anything wired to your skin must run on batteries and must never be connected to mains-
powered gear (a plugged-in laptop, a bench scope, a wall adapter) while electrodes are
on a body. Use series resistors in every electrode lead, and isolate (Bluetooth, or an
unplugged battery laptop) if you need to see the data on a computer. Everything in this
guide only measures — never build anything that pushes current into a person, and do not
attach electrodes to anyone with a pacemaker or implanted device.

unplugged battery laptop) if you need to see the data on a computer. Everything in this
guide only measures — never build anything that pushes current into a person, and do not
attach electrodes to anyone with a pacemaker or implanted device.

firmwareCode:
// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

evidenceBlocks.claim: Principio físico y lógico de Single-Channel Alpha-Wave EEG Monitor.
evidenceBlocks.textSnippet:
Why not just notch out the mains hum and skip the fancy front end? A notch filter removes
interference after the amplifier — but if the hum is a thousand times larger than the
signal, it has already saturated your gain stages and the ECG is unrecoverable. And a notch
near the QRS band distorts the waveform. The real fix is rejecting the interference at the
input, with CMRR and a driven reference, so it never gets amplified in the first place.

firmwareCode:
// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

firmwareCode:
// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

This is the build that makes people stop scrolling. Take the EMG envelope from project 4, map
it to servo positions, and a tendon-driven robotic hand opens and closes in time with your
own muscle — the same myoelectric principle behind real prosthetic limbs. Add a second EMG
channel (flexor and extensor) and you can command open and close independently; map the
envelope proportionally and the grip strength follows your effort. It ties every skill in
this guide together into a single, visceral demo: biology in, mechanics out.

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You can take a noisy biological signal all the way through a real system —
amplification, filtering, envelope extraction, calibration, thresholding, and actuator
control — and make it work in real time on a living body. That end-to-end biosignal-to-
actuator pipeline is exactly what prosthetics and neural-interface teams build.

this guide together into a single, visceral demo: biology in, mechanics out.

firmwareCode:
// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

description.whatDoesItDo:
! THE RULES, EVERY SINGLE TIME
Battery power only. Never connect a body-attached circuit to mains-powered equipment —
no plugged-in laptop, no bench scope, no wall adapter. Put current-limiting resistors in
every electrode lead, and isolate (Bluetooth, or a laptop running on battery) if you
need the data on a computer. Everything here only measures; never build anything that
pushes current into a person, and never attach electrodes to anyone with a pacemaker or
implanted device. And none of these are medical devices — they are demonstrations, and
no health decision should ever come from one.

evidenceBlocks.textSnippet:
EEG is the hardest biosignal there is: tens of microvolts, a hundred times smaller than an
ECG, buried under mains hum, muscle tension, and eye movement. But there is one effect a
careful DIY rig can genuinely capture — the alpha rhythm. Relax with your eyes closed and an
8 to 12 Hz oscillation appears over the back of your head; open your eyes and it vanishes
within a second. Watching that band power rise and fall on an FFT, on command, is the most
demanding and most rewarding build in this guide — and it is a real, reproducible
neuroscience result, not a gimmick.

firmwareCode:
// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

photodiode and you have a beam; break it and a voltage collapses in microseconds. Put two
beams a known distance apart, time how long an object takes to cross from one to the other,

cheapest possible photonics build, the response is instant and visual, and it teaches the
photodetection front end that every later project in this guide depends on.

firmwareCode:
// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

description.purpose:
Time-of-flight, literally: The sensor emits a short IR pulse and measures the round-trip
time t to the target. Distance = c·t/2. Light travels ~30 cm per nanosecond, so the timing
must be picosecond-class — which is why it lives inside a dedicated chip, not your Arduino.

description.whatDoesItDo:
Radar measures distance with radio; LiDAR does it with light. A time-of-flight sensor fires a
pulse of infrared light, measures how long it takes to bounce back, and multiplies by the
speed of light to get range — millimetre-accurate, dozens of times a second. Building one
around a module like the VL53L1X gets you a working laser rangefinder in an afternoon, and

evidenceBlocks.textSnippet:
Radar measures distance with radio; LiDAR does it with light. A time-of-flight sensor fires a
pulse of infrared light, measures how long it takes to bounce back, and multiplies by the
speed of light to get range — millimetre-accurate, dozens of times a second. Building one
around a module like the VL53L1X gets you a working laser rangefinder in an afternoon, and
understanding what it does underneath — pulse timing versus phase, the speed of light, photon
statistics — is the foundation of every autonomous-vehicle and robotics perception stack.
This is the headline build, and it feeds straight into the scanner in project 3.

firmwareCode:
// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

and plot the result — the outline of your room appears as a 2D point cloud, exactly like the
LiDAR on a robot vacuum or the spinning sensor on an early self-driving car. This is the most
visual build in the guide and the bridge from “I measured a distance” to “I perceived a
space,” which is the heart of robot navigation and SLAM.

// Firmware Receptor & Decodificador SDR (Python / GNU Radio)
import sys
import numpy as np
from rtlsdr import RtlSdr

sdr = RtlSdr()
sdr.sample_rate = 2.4e6    # 2.4 MSPS tasa de muestreo
sdr.center_freq = 1090e6   # Frecuencia transpondedor ADS-B (1090 MHz)
sdr.gain = 44.5            # Ganancia LNA en dB

print(f"[RADIO] Sintonizado en {sdr.center_freq / 1e6} MHz con ganancia {sdr.gain} dB.")

try:
    while True:
        # Lectura de muestras complejas I/Q (In-phase / Quadrature)
        samples = sdr.read_samples(256 * 1024)
        # Cálculo de potencia espectral instantánea (Magnitud IQ)
        magnitude = np.abs(samples)
        peak = np.max(magnitude)
        
        # Detección de preámbulo de pulso (Mode S squitter)
        if peak > 0.85:
            print(f"[ALERTA RF] Pulso detectado: Pico {peak:.2f} | Muestras > umbral: {np.sum(magnitude > 0.7)}")
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    sdr.close()
    print("[RADIO] Transceptor cerrado correctamente.")

firmwareCode:
// Firmware de Captura & Renderizado para Visor NoIR
import cv2
import time
from picamera2 import Picamera2

picam2 = Picamera2()
config = picam2.create_video_configuration(main={"size": (800, 600), "format": "XBGR8888"})
picam2.configure(config)

# Ajuste para sensibilidad ultra-baja en luz infrarroja
picam2.set_controls({
    "AnalogueGain": 16.0,          # Ganancia analógica máxima
    "ExposureTime": 33333,         # 33ms (30 FPS estables)
    "AwbEnable": False,            # Desactivar balance de blancos automático
    "ColourGains": (1.0, 1.0)
})

picam2.start()
cv2.namedWindow("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN)
cv2.setWindowProperty("NightVision", cv2.WND_PROP_FULLSCREEN, cv2.WINDOW_FULLSCREEN)

print("[SISTEMA] Visor nocturno activo. Presiona 'q' para salir.")
while True:
    frame = picam2.capture_array()
    # Procesamiento para maximizar contraste en oscuridad
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(frame, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=3.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8))
    enhanced = clahe.apply(gray)
    cv2.imshow("NightVision", enhanced)
    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        break

picam2.stop()
cv2.destroyAllWindows()

shape. Sweep the line across the object and you reconstruct a full 3D model, the same
structured-light principle behind many 3D scanners and depth cameras. It is the most
ambitious optical build here and a direct lesson in the camera-plus-light geometry at the
core of 3D vision.
